mainEntity.name: What is a class in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: A class in Java is a blueprint or template that defines the structure and behavior of objects. It specifies what data (fields/attributes) an object holds and what actions (methods) it can perform. A class itself is not an object — it is the definition from which objects are created. Syntax: class ClassName { // fields; // constructors; // methods; }. Think of a class like an architectural blueprint: the blueprint describes the house, but the actual house you live in is the object created from that blueprint.

mainEntity.name: What is an object in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: An object in Java is a runtime instance of a class. It is created using the 'new' keyword and allocated in heap memory. Each object has its own copy of instance fields (state) but shares the class's methods (behavior). Syntax: ClassName obj = new ClassName(); Every object has three characteristics: Identity (unique memory address), State (current values of its fields), and Behavior (methods it can invoke). For example, if 'Car' is a class, then 'Car myCar = new Car();' creates one specific car object with its own color, speed, and fuel level.

mainEntity.name: What is a constructor in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: A constructor in Java is a special method that is automatically called when an object is created with 'new'. It has the same name as the class and no return type (not even void). Its primary purpose is to initialize the object's fields. Java provides a no-argument default constructor automatically if you don't define any constructor. Types: (1) Default constructor — no parameters, (2) Parameterized constructor — accepts arguments for initialization, (3) Copy constructor — takes another object of the same class to create a copy. Constructors can be overloaded (multiple constructors with different parameter lists).

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between instance variables and static variables in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Instance variables belong to each individual object — every object gets its own separate copy. They represent the unique state of that object (e.g., a Car object's color, speed). Static variables belong to the class itself — all objects share one single copy. They represent shared state across all instances (e.g., total number of cars created). Instance variables are declared without 'static'; static variables use the 'static' keyword. Access: instance variables via object reference (obj.field); static variables via class name (ClassName.field). Static variables are initialized when the class is loaded; instance variables when an object is created.

mainEntity.name: What is the 'this' keyword in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: The 'this' keyword in Java is a reference to the current object — the object on which a method or constructor is being called. Primary uses: (1) Resolve naming conflict between instance fields and constructor/method parameters: 'this.name = name' when both are called 'name'. (2) Call another constructor of the same class: 'this(arg1, arg2)' — must be the first statement. (3) Pass the current object as a method argument. (4) Return the current object from a method (used in method chaining/builder pattern). 'this' cannot be used in static methods because static methods don't belong to any specific object.

sections.title: What are Classes and Objects in Java?

blocks.text: Java is a class-based, object-oriented programming (OOP) language — meaning everything in Java revolves around classes and objects. A class is a blueprint or template that defines the structure (data/fields) and behavior (methods) that its objects will have. An object is a specific, concrete instance created from that class blueprint, occupying memory and holding actual data values.

Real-world analogy: Think of a class as the architectural blueprint of a house — it describes how many rooms there are, where the doors go, and what the plumbing layout looks like. An object is an actual house built from that blueprint. You can build many different houses (objects) from the same blueprint (class), and each house can have different paint colors and furniture (field values), but they all share the same structural design (class definition).

In Java, every program has at least one class. Even the Hello World program is wrapped in a class. Objects are created at runtime using the new keyword, which allocates memory in the heap and calls a constructor to initialize the object's state. Without classes and objects, there is no Java program.

blocks.title: 🔑 Java Classes & Objects at a Glance
blocks.text: Key concepts: (1) Class — blueprint with fields, constructors, and methods. (2) Object — runtime instance created with 'new'. (3) Constructor — special method that initializes a new object. (4) Field — variable that holds object state. (5) Method — function that defines object behavior. (6) Access Modifier — controls visibility (public, private, protected, default). (7) static — belongs to the class, not any specific object. (8) this — reference to the current object instance.

A class declaration defines a new reference type in Java. It specifies the class name, optional modifiers, the fields (data) the class holds, the constructors used to create objects, and the methods (behavior) objects can perform. The class body is enclosed in curly braces {}. By convention, class names use PascalCase (e.g., BankAccount, StudentRecord).

items.title: Class Syntax
Class Rules
items.text:
1. Class name must match the filename exactly (for public classes).
2. One public class per .java file.
3. Class names use PascalCase — BankAccount, not bankaccount.
4. Fields should be private (encapsulation); methods can be public.
5. Every class implicitly extends java.lang.Object if no parent is specified.

items.title: Class Components
items.text: Fields: store object data (int age, String name). Constructors: initialize objects when 'new' is used. Methods: define what objects can do. Access modifiers: control who can see each member. Static members: belong to the class itself, not individual objects.

blocks.label: BankAccount.java
lines: // ── Static field — shared across ALL BankAccount objects ──
totalAccounts++;   // increment shared counter on each new object
System.out.println("Withdrawal denied — insufficient funds or minimum balance breach.");
// ── Static method — belongs to class, not any object ──

blocks.title: ⚠️ One Public Class Per File
blocks.text: A .java file can contain multiple classes, but only ONE can be declared 'public', and it MUST match the filename exactly. If your file is 'BankAccount.java', only 'public class BankAccount' is allowed as the public class. Other classes in the same file must not be public. Violating this causes a compile-time error: 'class X is public, should be declared in a file named X.java'.

Objects are created at runtime using the new keyword. The new keyword does three things in sequence: (1) Allocates memory in the heap for the new object, (2) Calls the constructor to initialize the object's fields, and (3) Returns a reference (memory address) to the newly created object, which is stored in a reference variable. The reference variable itself lives on the stack; the object lives on the heap.

blocks.label: ObjectCreation.java
lines: // ✅ Each object has its OWN copy of instance fields
// ✅ Static field — shared across all objects
// ✅ Reference variable stores ADDRESS of object, not the object itself
BankAccount ref1 = account1;  // ref1 and account1 point to SAME object
ref1.deposit(1000.0);         // modifies the same account1 object
// ✅ null reference — variable exists but points to no object
// emptyRef.deposit(100);  // ❌ NullPointerException — no object to call on
// ✅ Anonymous object — created without storing reference (used once)
// Object is immediately eligible for garbage collection after this line

blocks.title: 💡 Reference vs Object — Critical Distinction
blocks.text: A reference variable stores the MEMORY ADDRESS of an object, not the object itself. When you write 'BankAccount a = b', you are NOT copying the object — both 'a' and 'b' now point to the SAME object in heap memory. Changes through either reference affect the same object. To get a true copy, you must implement a copy constructor or override clone(). This is one of the most common sources of bugs for Java beginners.

A constructor is a special block of code that is automatically invoked when an object is created with new. It has the same name as the class and no return type — not even void. Constructors initialize the new object's fields to meaningful starting values. Java allows constructor overloading — multiple constructors with different parameter lists — so objects can be created in different ways depending on available information.

blocks.label: ConstructorTypes.java
lines: public Student(String name, int age, String course, double gpa) {
System.out.println("Single-arg constructor — chained to partial constructor");
Student s3 = new Student("Rohan", 21, "Computer Sci", 8.7); // Full

blocks.title: ⚠️ Default Constructor Disappears When You Define Your Own
blocks.text: Java provides a free no-argument default constructor ONLY if you define NO constructors at all. The moment you define even ONE constructor (e.g., a parameterized one), Java's automatic default constructor is removed. Calling 'new Student()' would then cause a compile error unless you explicitly define a no-arg constructor. Best practice: always explicitly define a no-arg constructor if you also define parameterized constructors, so clients can create objects either way.

blocks.title: 📌 this() — Constructor Chaining Rule
blocks.text: When using this() to call another constructor of the same class, it MUST be the very first statement in the constructor body. You cannot have any code before this(). Similarly, super() (calling parent class constructor) must be the first statement. You cannot use both this() and super() in the same constructor. Constructor chaining is a powerful way to reduce duplicate initialization code.

sections.title: Fields and Methods — State and Behavior

blocks.text: Fields (also called instance variables or attributes) define the state of an object — the data it holds. Methods define the behavior of an object — the actions it can perform. Together, fields and methods form the complete definition of what a class represents and can do. Good class design keeps fields private and exposes behavior through well-named public methods.

items.title: Instance Fields
items.text: Declared inside the class but outside any method. Each object gets its own independent copy. Example: 'private String name;' — every Student object has its own name. Default values: numeric fields default to 0, boolean to false, object references to null. Always declare fields private to enforce encapsulation.

items.title: Static Fields (Class Variables)
items.text: Declared with 'static' keyword. ONE copy shared across ALL objects of the class. Example: 'private static int totalStudents = 0;' — all Student objects share this counter. Used for: counters, constants (static final), shared configuration. Access via class name: 'Student.totalStudents', not via object reference.

items.title: Instance Methods
items.text: Called on a specific object — 'account.deposit(500)'. Can access and modify instance fields of the object. Have implicit access to 'this'. Most regular class methods are instance methods. Named with camelCase verbs: deposit(), withdraw(), calculateInterest(), getBalance().

items.title: Static Methods
items.text: Declared with 'static'. Belong to the class — called as 'ClassName.method()'. Cannot access instance fields or 'this' — they have no object context. Used for: utility functions (Math.sqrt()), factory methods, helper operations that don't need object state. main() is static because JVM calls it before any object exists.

items.title: Return Types
items.text: Methods return data using 'return statement'. Return type declared before method name: 'public double getBalance()' returns a double. 'public void deposit()' returns nothing. A method can return any type: primitives (int, double), objects (String, List), or void. The returned value can be used by the caller.

items.title: Parameters & Arguments
items.text: Parameters are variables in the method signature: 'public void deposit(double amount)'. Arguments are the actual values passed when calling: 'account.deposit(5000.0)'. Java is PASS BY VALUE — primitives pass a copy of the value; objects pass a copy of the reference (not the object itself). Modifying a primitive parameter inside a method doesn't affect the caller.

blocks.label: FieldsAndMethods.java
lines: // ── Static field — shared by all circles ──
public  static final double PI = 3.141592653589793; // constant
// Cannot use 'this.radius' here — no object context in static method
System.out.println("c1 larger than c2? " + c1.isLargerThan(c2)); // false

blocks.text: Access modifiers in Java control the visibility and accessibility of classes, fields, constructors, and methods. They are a core mechanism of encapsulation — one of the four pillars of OOP. Java has four access levels: public, protected, default (package-private), and private. Choosing the right modifier prevents unauthorized access to internal data and implementation details.

blocks.label: AccessModifiers.java
lines: public    String publicName;    // Accessible from anywhere
protected int    protectedAge;  // Accessible in same package + subclasses
String defaultEmail;  // Accessible only within same package (no keyword)
private   double privateSalary; // Accessible only within this class
public Person(String name, int age, String email, double salary) {
// ✅ Public method — part of the class's public API
System.out.println("Hi, I am " + publicName + ", age " + protectedAge);
// ✅ Private helper — internal implementation detail, hidden from outside
// ✅ Public method that internally uses private helper
return privateSalary - calculateTax(); // internal use is fine

blocks.title: 💡 Golden Rule of Access Modifiers
blocks.text: Always apply the MOST RESTRICTIVE access level that still works. Start with private — make something more visible only when there is a clear, justified reason. Fields: almost always private. Internal helper methods: private. Methods that form the class API: public. Methods needed only by subclasses: protected. This approach is called 'principle of least privilege' and prevents unintended coupling between classes.

The this keyword in Java is a reference to the current object — the specific object on which the current method or constructor is being executed. It is used to disambiguate between instance fields and local variables with the same name, to call other constructors of the same class, to pass the current object as an argument, and to return the current object (method chaining). this is only available in non-static contexts.

blocks.label: ThisKeyword.java
lines: // ── Use 1: Disambiguate field vs parameter (most common use) ──
public Employee(String name, String department, double salary) {
// ── Use 2: Constructor chaining — this() calls another constructor ──
// ── Use 3: Pass current object as argument ──
return this; // returns current object for chaining
// ❌ this cannot be used in static method
// In a static context: System.out.println(this); // COMPILE ERROR

sections.title: Static vs Instance Members — Class-Level vs Object-Level

blocks.text: One of the most important distinctions in Java OOP is between static members (class-level) and instance members (object-level). Static members are declared with the static keyword and belong to the class — they exist independently of any object. Instance members belong to each individual object — they are created fresh for every new object. Confusing the two is a very common source of bugs.

rows: ❌ No — no object context in static
✅ Yes — full access to instance fields
❌ No — cannot access instance fields directly
When the class is first loaded by JVM
When the class is unloaded (program end)
Shared data: counters, constants, utility methods

blocks.label: StaticVsInstance.java
lines: // ── Instance variable — each object has its own count ──
// ── Static variable — ONE shared count for ALL objects ──
instanceCount++;  // only this object's count goes up
staticCount++;    // the shared class-wide count goes up
// ✅ Static utility method — no object needed
// return instanceCount; // ❌ COMPILE ERROR — no instance context

blocks.text: Encapsulation is one of the four pillars of object-oriented programming. It means bundling data (fields) and behavior (methods) together in a class, while hiding the internal state from outside access. In Java, encapsulation is achieved by declaring fields private and providing controlled access through public getter and setter methods. This gives the class full control over how its data is read or modified — allowing validation, transformation, and protection of internal state.

blocks.label: Encapsulation.java
lines: // ✅ Private fields — hidden from outside; only accessible via methods
public Product(String name, double price, int stockQuantity, String category) {
setName(name);              // use setter for validation even in constructor
// ── Setter with validation: cannot set blank name ──
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Product name cannot be blank");
// ── Setter with validation: price must be positive ──
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Price cannot be negative");
if (qty < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Stock cannot be negative");
// ── Read-only field — no setter for category (set once at construction) ──

blocks.title: 💡 Encapsulation Benefits — Why Private Fields Matter
blocks.text: Without encapsulation, any code anywhere could set 'product.price = -9999' or 'student.age = -5' — invalid states that break your program logic. With private fields and setter validation, the class acts as a gatekeeper: impossible states can never be set. Additional benefits: (1) Internal implementation can change without breaking callers. (2) Debugging is easier — invalid state can only be set in one place. (3) Thread safety is easier to achieve. (4) The public API is clearly defined.

Understanding how Java manages memory for objects is critical for writing correct code and avoiding NullPointerException. Java memory is divided into two main areas: the Stack stores method call frames and local variables (including reference variables), and the Heap stores all object instances. The Garbage Collector (GC) automatically reclaims heap memory from objects that are no longer referenced.

items.title: Stack Memory
items.text: Stores: method call frames, local variables, primitive values, and object REFERENCES (addresses). LIFO structure — last in, first out. Fast access. Size is limited. When a method returns, its stack frame is popped. Reference variables live on the stack; the objects they point to live on the heap. Thread-safe — each thread has its own stack.

items.title: Heap Memory
items.text: Where ALL objects are stored — created with 'new'. Shared across all threads. Much larger than stack. Objects stay alive as long as at least one reference points to them. Managed by Garbage Collector — GC periodically scans for unreferenced objects and frees their memory. Setting a reference to null removes that reference; if no other references exist, the object becomes eligible for GC.

items.title: Garbage Collection
items.text: Java's automatic memory management. GC runs in the background, finding objects with no live references and reclaiming their heap memory. Developers don't need to manually free memory (unlike C/C++). An object becomes GC-eligible when: all reference variables pointing to it are set to null, go out of scope, or are reassigned. GC call is not guaranteed immediately: 'System.gc()' is a hint, not a command.

items.title: NullPointerException
items.text: Thrown when you call a method or access a field on a null reference — a reference variable that doesn't point to any object. Example: 'Student s = null; s.getName();' — NPE! Prevention: always initialize references before use, check for null before calling methods, use Optional<T> for values that might be absent. Java 14+ NPEs have helpful messages showing exactly which reference was null.

blocks.label: ObjectMemory.java
lines: // ── Stack: reference variable 'a' | Heap: Student object ──
Student a = new Student("Arjun", 22);  // 'a' is on stack, object on heap
// ── Stack: reference variable 'b' | SAME heap object as 'a' ──
Student b = a;  // b copies the REFERENCE (address), not the object
b.setName("Bhavna");   // modifies the SAME object that 'a' points to
// ── Make 'a' point to a NEW object ──
a = new Student("Chetan", 25); // new object in heap; old object now has only 'b' pointing to it
// ── Set b to null — original object now has NO references ──
b = null; // Original 'Bhavna' object is now GC-eligible
// ── Anonymous object — no reference stored, GC-eligible immediately ──
new Student("Temp", 18).display(); // used and immediately eligible for GC
System.gc(); // Hint to JVM to run GC — not guaranteed to run immediately

sections.title: Common Mistakes & Pitfalls — Bugs That Fool Everyone

blocks.text: These mistakes appear repeatedly in beginner Java code related to classes and objects. Each one can cause subtle bugs that are hard to trace. Study them carefully to recognize them in your own code.

blocks.label: CommonMistakes.java
lines: // ❌ MISTAKE 1: Accessing instance member from static method
// Cannot make a static reference to the non-static field 'model'
// Fix: either make method non-static, or accept a Car parameter
// ❌ MISTAKE 2: Forgetting 'this' — field shadowed by parameter
width = width; // ❌ Assigns parameter to itself — field never set!
// ❌ MISTAKE 3: Assuming reference copy = object copy
Student s2 = s1;      // ❌ s2 is NOT a copy — both point to SAME object
// Fix: implement a copy constructor: Student s2 = new Student(s1);
// ❌ MISTAKE 4: Calling method on uninitialized reference
// Fix: always initialize before use, or add null check
// ❌ MISTAKE 5: Adding return type to constructor
// public void MyClass() { }  // ❌ This is a METHOD named 'MyClass', not a constructor!
// Java silently treats it as a regular method — the real constructor is never called
// Fix: constructors have NO return type: public MyClass() { }
// ❌ MISTAKE 6: Using == to compare objects instead of .equals()
if (s1 == s2) {        // ❌ FALSE — different objects in heap
// ❌ MISTAKE 7: Accessing static member via object reference (misleading)
c1.staticCount; // ❌ Misleading — looks like instance access
// Fix: Counter.staticCount — use class name for static members

sections.title: Java 21 Records — Compact, Immutable Data Classes

blocks.text: Java 16 introduced Records (JEP 395) as a permanent feature — a special, compact class form designed for immutable data carriers. A record automatically generates: a canonical constructor, private final fields, public getter methods (named after the field, without 'get' prefix), toString(), equals(), and hashCode(). Records eliminate the boilerplate of traditional POJO (Plain Old Java Object) classes when all you need is to store and pass data.

blocks.label: JavaRecords.java
lines: // ❌ BEFORE Records: Traditional POJO — 40+ lines of boilerplate
public PointOld(double x, double y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }
@Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(x, y); }
@Override public String toString() { return "Point[x=" + x + ", y=" + y + "]"; }
// ✅ AFTER Records: Same thing in 1 line — Java 16+
// Automatically generated: constructor, x(), y(), equals(), hashCode(), toString()
record Product(String name, double price, int stock) {
// Compact constructor — no parameter list needed here
if (name == null || name.isBlank()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Name required");
if (price < 0)  throw new IllegalArgumentException("Price cannot be negative");
if (stock < 0)  throw new IllegalArgumentException("Stock cannot be negative");
name = name.trim(); // can normalize fields in compact constructor
public double discountedPrice(double pct) { return price * (1 - pct / 100); }
// Records are IMMUTABLE — no setters; fields are final

blocks.title: 💡 When to Use Records vs Regular Classes
blocks.text: Use Records when: the class is a pure data carrier (DTO, value object, response payload), all fields should be immutable (set once, never changed), and you want equals/hashCode based on all fields automatically. Use regular classes when: objects need mutable state (setters that change values), the class has complex behavior beyond storing data, inheritance is needed (records cannot extend other classes, though they can implement interfaces), or you need different equals/hashCode logic.

sections.title: Bad Practices & Anti-Patterns — What Senior Developers Reject

blocks.text: These class and object anti-patterns are the most common reasons for failed code reviews in professional Java teams. Each reduces maintainability, testability, or correctness.

items.title: God Class (Doing Too Much)
items.text: A class with hundreds of fields and methods that handles everything — database access, business logic, UI rendering, email sending — in one giant class. Violates the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP). Fix: decompose into focused classes: CustomerService, CustomerRepository, EmailNotifier. Each class should have ONE reason to change.

items.title: Public Fields (Breaking Encapsulation)
items.text: Declaring fields as public: 'public int balance;' — any code anywhere can set 'account.balance = -1000000;' — an impossible valid state. Always make fields private and provide validated getters/setters. Public fields make refactoring impossible — you can never change the type or add validation later without breaking all callers.

items.title: Mutable Static Fields (Global State)
items.text: Static mutable fields behave like global variables — any code can modify them, causing unpredictable behavior, especially in multithreaded environments. Every test that changes a static field can affect all subsequent tests. Use static only for constants (static final) or counters that are intentionally shared. Prefer dependency injection over static state.

items.title: Anemic Domain Model
items.text: Classes with only getters and setters and no real behavior — just data bags. All business logic lives in separate 'Service' classes that pull data out, manipulate it, and push it back. This defeats the purpose of OOP. Move behavior that naturally belongs to the class INTO the class: instead of 'accountService.isOverdrawn(account)', write 'account.isOverdrawn()' directly in the Account class.

items.title: Missing toString() and equals()/hashCode()
items.text: Not overriding toString() means debugging shows 'com.example.Student@1b6d3586' — useless. Not overriding equals() means object comparison uses reference equality — two Student objects with the same ID won't be equal in collections. Always override toString() for debuggability and equals()+hashCode() together for objects used in collections (List, Map, Set). Records do this automatically.

items.title: Excessive Constructor Parameters
items.text: A constructor with 8-10 parameters is a sign the class is doing too much OR needs a Builder pattern. 'new User(name, email, phone, address, age, role, status, createdDate, lastLogin, preferredLanguage)' — callers can't remember the order. Fix: use the Builder pattern for complex object construction, or split into smaller focused classes.

blocks.label: AntiPatterns.java
lines: public double balance;  // ❌ Anyone can set account.balance = -999999
// ✅ BETTER: Private fields with validated access
if (balance < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Balance cannot be negative");
System.out.println(s); // ❌ Prints: Student@7852e922 — useless for debugging
// ❌ ANTI-PATTERN 4: Anemic class — no behavior, just data
// All logic in OrderService — order knows nothing about itself
// ✅ BETTER: Rich domain class with behavior

sections.title: Java Classes & Objects Interview Questions — Beginner to Advanced

blocks.text: These questions are consistently asked in Java fresher interviews, OCPJP certification exams, and campus placement tests for OOP topics.

items.q: Q1. What is the difference between a class and an object in Java?
items.a: A class is a blueprint or template — a compile-time construct that defines the structure (fields) and behavior (methods) of objects. It exists in source code and consumes no heap memory by itself. An object is a runtime instance created from the class blueprint using 'new'. Each object occupies heap memory and has its own copy of instance fields. Analogy: if 'Car' is a class (the blueprint), then 'Car myCar = new Car()' creates one specific Car object (an actual car). You can create many objects from one class, each with different field values but sharing the same methods.

items.q: Q2. What is a constructor in Java? How is it different from a method?
items.a: A constructor is a special code block that runs automatically when an object is created with 'new'. Key differences from methods: (1) Name: constructor must have the SAME name as the class; methods have any name. (2) Return type: constructors have NO return type — not even void; methods must declare a return type. (3) Invocation: constructors are called automatically by 'new'; methods are called explicitly on objects. (4) Purpose: constructors initialize object state; methods define object behavior. (5) Inheritance: constructors are NOT inherited; methods are. If you accidentally add a void return type to a constructor, Java treats it as a regular method — the real constructor is never provided (unless a default one exists).

items.q: Q3. What is the difference between static and instance variables?
items.a: Instance variables: declared without 'static', belong to each individual object, each object gets its own separate copy, initialized when 'new' creates the object, accessed via object reference (obj.field). Static variables: declared with 'static', belong to the CLASS itself, ONE copy shared across ALL objects, initialized when the class is first loaded by JVM, accessed via class name (ClassName.field). Example: 'private String name' is an instance variable — every Student has their own name. 'private static int totalStudents' is a static variable — one counter for all students. Modifying a static variable through one object affects what all other objects see, because they all share the same copy.

items.q: Q4. Can we have multiple constructors in a Java class? What is constructor overloading?
items.a: Yes — a class can have multiple constructors, each with a different parameter list. This is called constructor overloading. Java distinguishes overloaded constructors by the number, types, and order of parameters. Example: Student(), Student(String name), Student(String name, int age), Student(String name, int age, String course) — four constructors for the same class. The appropriate constructor is selected at compile time based on the arguments passed to 'new'. Constructor chaining: one constructor can call another of the same class using 'this(args)' as the very first statement — avoiding duplicate initialization code.

items.q: Q5. What is encapsulation and how is it implemented in Java?
items.a: Encapsulation is the OOP principle of bundling data and behavior in a class while hiding internal state from outside access. In Java, it is implemented by: (1) Declaring all fields private — no outside code can access them directly. (2) Providing public getter methods to allow controlled reading of field values. (3) Providing public setter methods with validation to allow controlled modification. Benefits: invalid states can never be set (validation in setters), internal implementation can change without affecting callers, the public API is clearly defined, debugging is easier (invalid state has one entry point). A class with public fields is NOT encapsulated — any code can set any value, including impossible ones.

items.q: Q6. What is the 'this' keyword in Java and where can it be used?
items.a: 'this' is a reference to the current object — the object on which the current method or constructor is executing. Four main uses: (1) Disambiguation: 'this.name = name' when both field and parameter are named 'name'. (2) Constructor chaining: 'this(arg1, arg2)' calls another constructor of the same class — must be the first statement. (3) Passing current object: 'registry.add(this)' passes the current object as an argument. (4) Method chaining: 'return this' allows fluent/builder-style calls like 'employee.setDepartment("IT").setSalary(50000)'. RESTRICTION: 'this' cannot be used in static methods — static methods have no object context and 'this' would have nothing to refer to.

items.q: Q7. What happens when you do 'Student s2 = s1'? Is this a copy of the object?
items.a: No — this is NOT a copy of the object. Both s1 and s2 now hold the SAME memory address, pointing to the SAME object in the heap. Changes made through s2 are visible through s1 and vice versa — because they are the same object, not two separate ones. To create a true independent copy: (1) Implement a copy constructor: 'Student s2 = new Student(s1)' — copy constructor manually copies all field values into a new object. (2) Override clone() and implement Cloneable. (3) Use serialization/deserialization for deep copies. This distinction between reference copy and object copy is one of the most important concepts in Java OOP.

items.q: Q8. What is the default constructor in Java? When does it disappear?
items.a: Java automatically provides a no-argument default constructor if — and ONLY if — you define NO constructors at all in the class. The default constructor has no parameters and does nothing (just calls super()). It disappears the moment you define even ONE constructor of your own. If you define a parameterized constructor 'Student(String name, int age)' and then call 'new Student()', you get a compile error — no matching constructor. Best practice: always explicitly define a no-arg constructor alongside any parameterized constructors, so objects can be created either way. Frameworks like JPA/Hibernate also require a no-arg constructor to create entity objects via reflection.

items.q: Q9. What are Java Records and when should you use them (Java 16+)?
items.a: A Record is a special compact class form in Java 16+ designed for immutable data carriers. Syntax: 'record Point(double x, double y) {}'. Java automatically generates: a canonical constructor, private final fields, public accessors (named x() and y(), not getX()), equals(), hashCode(), and toString(). Records are: (1) Immutable — fields are final, no setters. (2) Transparent — equals/hashCode based on all fields. (3) Concise — eliminates POJO boilerplate. Use records for: DTOs (Data Transfer Objects), API response/request models, value objects, coordinates/dimensions, any data you'd previously model as a 'dumb' class with just getters. Don't use records for: mutable data, classes requiring inheritance (records can't extend classes), or when you need different equals/hashCode logic.

items.q: Q10. What is the difference between stack and heap in Java object memory?
items.a: Stack: stores method call frames, local variables, and reference variables (object addresses). LIFO structure, fixed size, fast. Each thread has its own stack. When a method returns, its stack frame is removed. Heap: stores all object instances (created with 'new'). Shared across all threads. Much larger than stack. Managed by Garbage Collector — objects live in heap as long as at least one reference points to them. Practical implications: (1) Reference variable on stack holds ADDRESS of object on heap — not the object itself. (2) Assigning 'a = b' copies the address, not the object. (3) Setting a variable to null removes that reference — if no references remain, GC can collect the object. (4) NullPointerException happens when you call a method on a null reference — a variable that holds no address.

When 'd2.name = "Max"' is executed, it modifies the name field of that shared object. So d1.bark() and d2.bark() both print 'Max' — they operate on the same object. Key lesson: 'd2 = d1' is a reference copy, NOT an object copy.

Two bugs: (1) 'public void Rectangle(...)' — adding 'void' makes this a METHOD, not a constructor. Java silently compiles it as a method. The class has no explicit constructor, so Java provides a default no-arg constructor that doesn't set width or height. (2) 'width = width' and 'height = height' — missing 'this.' — the parameter is assigned to itself, not the field. Fix: remove 'void' and add 'this.': 'public Rectangle(int width, int height) { this.width = width; this.height = height; }'

items.q: 3. Design a 'Circle' class with: private field 'radius' (double), constructor that validates radius > 0 (throw IllegalArgumentException if not), methods calculateArea() and calculateCircumference(), and a proper toString().

4. A 'Counter' class has: 'private int count = 0;' and 'public static int totalCounters = 0;'. If you create Counter c1, c2, c3 and call c1.increment() twice, c2.increment() once, what is c1.count, c2.count, c3.count, and Counter.totalCounters?
items.a: Assuming increment() does 'count++; totalCounters++;': c1.count = 2 (incremented twice through c1), c2.count = 1 (incremented once through c2), c3.count = 0 (never incremented). Counter.totalCounters = 3 (shared across all — 2 from c1 + 1 from c2). This demonstrates the core difference: instance field 'count' is separate per object; static field 'totalCounters' is ONE shared copy that all objects modify together.

This demonstrates the key difference: instance fields are independent per object, static fields are shared.

sections.title: Conclusion — Classes & Objects: The Foundation of Every Java Program

blocks.text: Classes and objects are the foundation of Java. Every Java program is built from classes — even the simplest Hello World lives inside one. Understanding how classes define structure and behavior, how objects are created and live in heap memory, and how encapsulation protects data integrity is not just academic theory — it directly determines the quality of every line of Java code you write.

The difference between beginner and professional Java code is often visible in class design: beginners use public fields, forget encapsulation, create classes that do too much, and confuse reference copies for object copies. Professional Java code has private fields, validated setters, clearly named methods, single-responsibility classes, and meaningful toString()/equals()/hashCode() overrides.

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions — Java Classes and Objects

items.q: What is a class in Java?
items.a: A class in Java is a blueprint or template that defines the structure (fields/attributes) and behavior (methods) of objects. It is a compile-time construct — it defines what objects will look like, but is not itself an object occupying heap memory. Every Java program must have at least one class. By convention, class names use PascalCase (BankAccount, StudentRecord). One public class is allowed per .java file and its name must match the filename exactly.

items.q: What is an object in Java?
items.a: An object is a runtime instance of a class, created using the 'new' keyword. It occupies memory in the heap and holds actual data values in its instance fields. Each object has three characteristics: Identity (unique memory address), State (current field values), and Behavior (methods it can call). Multiple objects can be created from one class, each with independent state but sharing the same method definitions.

items.q: What is a constructor in Java?
items.a: A constructor is a special code block with the same name as the class and no return type. It executes automatically when 'new' creates an object, initializing the object's fields to meaningful starting values. Java provides a free default no-arg constructor only if you define no constructors at all. Constructors can be overloaded (multiple constructors with different parameter lists). Constructor chaining uses 'this(args)' to call another constructor — must be the first statement.

items.q: What is the difference between instance variables and static variables in Java?
items.a: Instance variables belong to each individual object — every object gets its own separate copy, representing unique object state (name, age, balance). Static variables belong to the class itself — all objects share one copy (totalStudents, TAX_RATE). Instance variables are declared without 'static'; static use the 'static' keyword. Access instance via object reference (obj.field); access static via class name (ClassName.field). Modifying a static variable through any object changes what all objects see.

items.q: What is the 'this' keyword in Java?
items.a: The 'this' keyword is a reference to the current object — the object on which the current method or constructor is executing. Main uses: (1) Disambiguate field vs parameter with the same name: 'this.name = name'. (2) Call another constructor: 'this(arg1, arg2)' — first statement only. (3) Pass current object as argument: 'registry.add(this)'. (4) Return current object for chaining: 'return this'. Cannot be used in static methods — static methods have no object context.
